notes:
Here are verse-by-verse notes on Isaiah 13, drawn from the sources I could access.

---

## ISAIAH 13 — VERSE-BY-VERSE NOTES

### v. 1 — "This is the burden against Babylon that Isaiah son of Amoz received"

**The word "burden" (Hebrew *massa'*):** Comes from a verb meaning "to lift up" (*nasa'*). It can mean either "oracle/utterance" (lifting up the voice) or "burden" (a heavy load). Both senses apply: this is a weighty message of judgment. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-13/) — Ellicott adds that the word acquired a half-technical sense as announcing the doom a nation was called to bear, and that "oracle" is perhaps the best English equivalent. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/13.htm) — Gill notes that the Targum renders it "the burden of the cup of cursing to give Babylon to drink." (https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/isaiah/13.htm)

**Who was this prophecy for?** Guzik (Enduring Word) stresses that this prophecy was probably never published in Babylon. It was given for the comfort of God's people — to assure Israel and Judah that God is just, that He would judge their enemies, and that His discipline of them was not arbitrary. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-13/) — Precept Austin quotes Young: the oracles were given so that "Israel would learn that God does not permit to go unpunished the wickedness of those who have set themselves against the Lord." (https://www.preceptaustin.org/isaiah_13_commentary)

**Timing:** Isaiah finished his prophetic career around 685 BC, nearly 100 years before Judah fell to Babylon (586 BC). At the time of this prophecy, Babylon was a significant nation but behind the Assyrian Empire in status. Yet God speaks of its judgment centuries in advance. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-13/)

---

### v. 2 — "Raise a banner on a barren hilltop; call aloud to them. Wave your hand, that they may enter the gates of the nobles."

**Summons to war:** God calls for a signal to be raised on a bare (treeless) mountain so the invading army can see it. The banner, the shout, and the waving hand are three ways of summoning the army that God is mustering against Babylon. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-13/) — Ellicott specifies "a bare mountain, where there were no trees to hide the standard." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/13.htm)

**"Gates of the nobles":** Ellicott says the phrase heightens the contrast between the greatness of the city — with gates that had witnessed the entrance of kings and princes for centuries — and the wild roughness of the barbarian destroyers. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/13.htm) — Gill notes an alternative reading: the soldiers rallying to the doors of the generals to enlist. (https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/isaiah/13.htm)

---

### v. 3 — "I have commanded My sanctified ones; I have even summoned My warriors to execute My wrath and exult in My triumph."

**"My sanctified ones":** Not holy in the spiritual sense, but consecrated or set apart by God for this specific task of judgment. Ellicott compares this to Cyrus being called "the anointed" of the Lord (Isaiah 45:1). The Medes and Persians are "sanctified" only in the sense of being appointed instruments. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/13.htm) — Gill says the same: "not because sanctified by the Spirit of God… but because they were set apart in the mind and counsel of God for a special work." (https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/isaiah/13.htm)

**"Exult in My triumph" (literally "rejoice in My highness"):** Gill interprets this as the invaders rejoicing that God is exalted through their work, or God rejoicing because He is glorified by them. (https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/isaiah/13.htm) — Ellicott notes the proud consciousness of the invaders that they are doing God's work. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/13.htm)

---

### v. 4 — "Listen, a tumult on the mountains, like that of a great multitude! … The LORD of Hosts is mobilizing an army for war."

The prophet hears the tramp of armies gathering on the mountains north of Babylonia — possibly the Zagros range or the plateau of Iran — before they descend to the plain. It is the LORD of Hosts Himself who musters them. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/13.htm) — Gill says this was fulfilled in Cyrus's army, which consisted of several kingdoms and nations (Medes, Persians, and peoples of Ararat, Minni, and Ashchenaz per Jeremiah 51:27). (https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/isaiah/13.htm) — Precept Austin notes that the phrase "the LORD of hosts musters the army" emphasizes God's sovereign control over history, even the darkest moments being under His providential rule. (https://www.preceptaustin.org/isaiah_13_commentary)

---

### v. 5 — "They are coming from faraway lands, from the ends of the heavens — the LORD and the weapons of His wrath — to destroy the whole country."

Both Media and Persia were far countries to the Hebrews. Ellicott says "from the end of heaven" represents the *ultima Thule* of the known world in Isaiah's day. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/13.htm) — The Pulpit Commentary (summarised in search results) notes the effective anthropomorphism: Jehovah Himself is portrayed as marching with the army He mustered. Gill says "the whole land" means the land of Chaldea specifically, not the whole world, though the Septuagint renders it "the whole earth." (https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/isaiah/13.htm)

---

### v. 6 — "Wail, for the Day of the LORD is near; it will come as destruction from the Almighty."

**"Day of the LORD":** Used about 26 times in Scripture. It speaks not of a single 24-hour day but of a season of judgment when God sets things right. Each "day of the Lord" in history (like the fall of Babylon) is a type of the final great Day. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-13/) — JFB calls it "day of His vengeance on Babylon" and a "type of the future 'day of wrath' (Revelation 6:17)." (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/jfb/isaiah/13.htm, accessed via search excerpt)

**"Destruction from the Almighty":** In Hebrew there is a striking assonance: *k'shod mish-Shaddai* ("destruction from the Destroyer"). *Shaddai* (Almighty) is an ancient name of God used rarely by the prophets (only here, Joel 1:15, and Ezekiel 1:24; 10:5). The Pulpit Commentary notes some scholars derive *Shaddai* from the Arabic word for "sender of storms," giving the sense "destruction from the Storm-Sender." (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/isaiah/13.htm, via search excerpt) — Ellicott says the assonance may be coupled with etymology: *Shaddai* being derived by many scholars from *shadad* = to destroy, giving "destruction from the Destroyer." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/13.htm)

**This verse is an almost verbal reproduction of Joel 1:15.** (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/13.htm)

---

### v. 7 — "Therefore all hands will fall limp, and every man's heart will melt."

Hands hanging down = helpless despondency. The recently discovered accounts of Babylon's capture by Cyrus show a great lack of activity and vigour on the part of the defenders, matching this description better than Herodotus's claim that the Babylonians felt secure within their walls. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/13.htm) — Gill: "they should not be able to lift them up to lay hold on a weapon, and defend themselves." (https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/isaiah/13.htm)

---

### v. 8 — "Terror, pain, and anguish will seize them; they will writhe like a woman in labor. They will look at one another, their faces flushed with fear."

**"Like a woman in labor":** A common biblical image for powerless agony (Hosea 13:3; Micah 5:9; Jeremiah 6:24; Psalm 48:6). (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/13.htm) — Guzik notes that when Babylon fell by Cyrus's clever surprise attack (see Daniel 5), the citizens were completely shocked — they were "amazed at one another." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-13/)

**"Faces flushed" (literally "faces like flames"):** Ellicott describes this as the moment when "the dejected pallor of ordinary fear flashes into a new intensity, and the eyeballs glare, and the face glows as with a terrible brightness." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/13.htm) — Gill notes an alternative reading: "their faces are as the faces of Lehabim" (Libyans) — i.e., black or tawny with distress and anguish (cf. Joel 2:6). (https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/isaiah/13.htm)

---

### v. 9 — "Behold, the Day of the LORD is coming — cruel, with fury and burning anger — to make the earth a desolation and to destroy the sinners within it."

Isaiah now speaks in the "prophetic tense" — seeing both near fulfillment (judgment on Babylon) and ultimate fulfillment (final judgment at Christ's return). (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-13/) — Guzik says "the day is 'cruel' not because God is cruel, but because the objects of His displeasure experience it as severe and painful." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-13/)

**"The earth" or "the land"?** The Hebrew *ha-arets* can mean either. The Pulpit Commentary notes that many critics would translate it "the earth" here, seeing the language go beyond Babylon to the wicked world of which Babylon is a type. But where context permits, restricting the meaning to "the land" (of Chaldea) seems better. (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/isaiah/13.htm, via search excerpt) — However, verses 9–13 clearly expand the scope.

---

### v. 10 — "For the stars of heaven and their constellations will not give their light. The rising sun will be darkened, and the moon will not give its light."

**Cosmic disturbances:** Several prophetic passages describe the darkening of sun, moon, and stars surrounding God's great judgments (Joel 2:10, 3:15; Revelation 6:12–14; Isaiah 34:4). Jesus Himself probably quotes or paraphrases this passage in Matthew 24:29. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-13/)

**Literal or figurative?** Gill takes this figuratively — expressing the horror and gloom of the judgment, as if the heavens themselves were frowning. The "stars" may symbolically represent kings, queens, and nobles. (https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/isaiah/13.htm) — Ellicott agrees: "It is obvious that the words in their first application had a figurative, and not a literal, fulfilment. Such imagery has been at all times the natural symbolism of a time of terror." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/13.htm) — Precept Austin, however, argues for a literal future fulfillment: "Isaiah describes major cosmic alterations in the sun, moon and stars, and this is something that has not yet occurred in the history of the world." Therefore the final fulfillment must be still future. (https://www.preceptaustin.org/isaiah_13_commentary)

**"Constellations" (Hebrew *kesil*):** This word is translated "Orion" in Job 9:9 and Amos 5:8. Ellicott notes a widely diffused ancient legend: the Persian name for the constellation was Nimrod, and the Arabian, "the Giant." In Greek mythology, Orion was a giant hunter notorious for outrages against the gods and finally slain by Zeus. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/13.htm) — Gill says the plural form (*kesilim*) may mean "were there ever so many Orions in the heavens, they should none of them give light." (https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/isaiah/13.htm)

---

### v. 11 — "I will punish the world for its evil and the wicked for their iniquity. I will end the haughtiness of the arrogant and lay low the pride of the ruthless."

Here the prophecy "certainly goes beyond the destruction of Babylon, and becomes a general warning to the wicked of all countries." (Ellicott — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/13.htm) — The punishment falls especially on arrogance, pride, and haughtiness — the characteristic sins of Babylon (cf. Nebuchadnezzar in Daniel 4:30 and Belshazzar in Daniel 5). Gill notes that the Babylonian rulers "Nebuchadnezzar and Belshazzar" were "famous for their pride, arrogance, and haughtiness." (https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/isaiah/13.htm)

Guzik ties this to Babylon as a biblical type: from the Tower of Babel (Genesis 11) onward, Babylon represents organized rebellion against God — the world system in opposition to Him that will be judged. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-13/)

---

### v. 12 — "I will make man scarcer than pure gold, and mankind rarer than the gold of Ophir."

**Population decimated:** The slaughter will be so great that human beings become rare and precious — like the purest gold (the gold of Ophir was proverbial for its preciousness: Job 22:24; 28:16; 1 Kings 9:28). (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/13.htm) — Ellicott notes that both Hebrew words for "man" used here (*enosh* and *adam*) express the frailty of human nature. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/13.htm)

Gill offers an alternative reading: the Medes would not be bribed by gold to spare anyone — they would not regard silver or gold (see v. 17), so a man could not be bought off even with the finest gold. (https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/isaiah/13.htm) — He also notes a Jewish interpretation applying this verse to the Messiah: "This is the Messiah, that shall ascend and be more precious than all the children of the world." (https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/isaiah/13.htm)

---

### v. 13 — "Therefore I will make the heavens tremble, and the earth will be shaken from its place at the wrath of the LORD of Hosts on the day of His burning anger."

**A great final shaking:** This echoes Haggai 2:6 ("Once more I will shake the heavens and the earth") and is quoted in Hebrews 12:25–28 regarding the final removal of all that can be shaken, so that only the unshakeable kingdom remains. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-13/)

**John Piper (Desiring God / Reformed Baptist)** preached on this verse: "There's coming a day, the Day of the Lord, of fierce anger and retribution and justice upon the earth for its sin, and the earth will be shaken out of its place." He connects it to the great final shaking when "this world is going to totter on its foundations someday and collapse as we know it." (https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/a-kingdom-that-cannot-be-shaken)

**Near or far fulfillment?** The Pulpit Commentary observes that Isaiah may "pass here from signs connected with the fall of Babylon to those which will announce the last day — each 'day of the Lord' being a type of the final and great day." (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/isaiah/13.htm, via search excerpt) — Guzik applies it pastorally: "Since God can shake the heavens and move the earth, and since God Himself is unshakable, it makes a lot more sense to trust in God than even the ground we stand on." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-13/)

Gill takes this figuratively: the shaking of heaven and earth describes the great confusion men would be in, "it being as if all nature was convulsed." (https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/isaiah/13.htm)

---

### v. 14 — "Like a hunted gazelle, like a sheep without a shepherd, each will return to his own people, each will flee to his native land."

**Foreigners flee:** When judgment falls on Babylon, the "mixed multitude" of all nations who had been brought into Babylon — whether as captives, traders, or pressed soldiers — will flee back to their homelands. The image of the hunted gazelle emphasizes unrelenting pursuit with no escape. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/13.htm) — This matches Jeremiah 50:16, which describes foreigners leaving Babylon when the sword of the oppressor comes.

Guzik sees a deeper application: "God's judgment, upon both Babylon and the world in general, is unrelenting. It is like a nature film where the hunted gazelle is overtaken by the lion, and is utterly consumed. There is no escape from God's unrelenting judgment." He adds that Jesus willingly became the hunted gazelle on the cross, bearing that same unrelenting judgment for us. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-13/)

---

### vv. 15–16 — "Whoever is caught will be stabbed … Their infants will be dashed to pieces before their eyes, their houses will be looted, and their wives will be ravished."

**Horrors of conquest:** These outrages were the standard, brutal accompaniments of a captured city in the ancient Near East. Ellicott notes that the words of v. 16 seem to have been in the minds of the exiles in Babylon when they uttered the dread beatitude of Psalm 137:9 ("Blessed is he who seizes your infants and dashes them against the rocks"). (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/13.htm)

Gill: "Every one that is found in the city of Babylon … shall be slain." The orders of Cyrus (according to historical accounts) were that those found in the streets should be killed. (https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/isaiah/13.htm)

---

### v. 17 — "Behold, I will stir up against them the Medes, who have no regard for silver and no desire for gold."

**The Medes named specifically:** This is a remarkable predictive detail. The Medes were a mixed people (Aryan conquerors mingled with an earlier Turanian race). Their name had recently come to Isaiah's notice through Shalmaneser's deportation of the Ten Tribes to "the cities of the Medes" (2 Kings 17:6). Ellicott notes that Isaiah names the Medes rather than the Persians probably because of their greater prominence at the time — just as the Greeks spoke of "the Mede" and used the term "Medism" for the Medo-Persian monarchy under Darius and Xerxes. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/13.htm)

**"No regard for silver … no desire for gold":** The Medes were too fierce to be bribed. They would take no ransom to stay their work of vengeance. Xenophon (*Cyropaedia* 5:3) represents Cyrus as acknowledging their unbought, unpaid service. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/13.htm) — Guzik notes that such specific prediction (naming the Medes centuries in advance) is what drives skeptics to claim Isaiah was written after the events, but "doesn't God know the future, and know it specifically?" (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-13/)

---

### v. 18 — "Their bows will dash young men to pieces; they will have no mercy on the fruit of the womb; they will not look with pity on the children."

Bows were the characteristic weapons of the Medo-Persian armies (cf. Isaiah 22:6; Jeremiah 1:9–14). The description of mercilessness — dashing young men, not sparing the unborn or children — paints the Medes as instruments of unrestrained divine wrath. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/13.htm)

---

### v. 19 — "And Babylon, the jewel of the kingdoms, the glory of the pride of the Chaldeans, will be overthrown by God like Sodom and Gomorrah."

**Babylon's former glory:** Even in Isaiah's time, Babylon impressed all who saw it. Nebuchadnezzar later exalted in it (Daniel 4:30). Herodotus described it as the most famous and strongest of all Assyrian cities, adorned beyond any other. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/13.htm)

**"Like Sodom and Gomorrah":** This phrase became proverbial for total destruction (Isaiah 1:9; Jeremiah 50:40; Deuteronomy 29:23). Guzik notes that "the phrase 'Sodom and Gomorrah' suggests not only complete destruction but also its moral cause" — Babylon's sin merited such judgment. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-13/)

**Fulfillment:** The work was accomplished gradually. Darius dismantled Babylon's walls, Xerxes pulled down the Temple of Belus. Alexander contemplated restoration but died early. By the time of Strabo (c. 20 BC), "the vast city" had become a "vast desolation." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/13.htm)

**Precept Austin argues that the final fulfillment is still future**, because Babylon has never been destroyed suddenly and completely "like Sodom and Gomorrah." The city was not devastated all at once but declined gradually — unlike Sodom's total overthrow. This supports the view that Babylon will one day be rebuilt and suffer a literal, cataclysmic future destruction (Rev 16:19; 17–18). (https://www.preceptaustin.org/isaiah_13_commentary)

---

### v. 20 — "She will never be inhabited or settled from generation to generation; no nomad will pitch his tent there, no shepherd will rest his flock there."

**Never inhabited again:** The ancient city of Babylon, once conquered, has never been reinhabited. Ellicott notes a remarkable literal fulfillment: "the Bedouins themselves, partly because the place is desolate, partly from a superstitious horror, shrink from encamping on the site of the ancient temples and palaces." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/13.htm) — Guzik: "When Cyrus conquered Babylon, he did not devastate the city. The walls were left standing until 518 BC, and general desolation did not set in until the third century BC. Babylon gradually fell into decay … Babylon became completely depopulated by the time of the Muslim conquest in the seventh century AD, and to this day it lies deserted." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-13/)

---

### vv. 21–22 — "But desert creatures will lie down there, and howling creatures will fill her houses. Ostriches will dwell there, and wild goats will leap about. Hyenas will howl in her fortresses and jackals in her luxurious palaces."

**Wild animals replace human habitation:** The exact animals are difficult to identify with certainty. Ellicott suggests: "wild beasts of the desert" = generic wild creatures; "doleful creatures" (literally "groaners") = probably horned owls; "owls" (literally "daughters of screaming") = ostriches (Job 39:13–18); "satyrs" (literally "hairy or shaggy ones") = either goats or a species of baboon still found in Babylonia; "wild beasts of the islands" = jackals or hyenas. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/13.htm)

Guzik adds: "The 'wild goats' (v. 21) are sometimes associated with demons in goat form that are called 'satyrs' (Leviticus 17:7; 2 Chronicles 11:15)." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-13/)

**"Babylon's time is at hand, and her days will not be prolonged":** Ellicott says this means "the appointed day of visitation" (cf. Jeremiah 46:21; 50:27). The whole passage finds a striking parallel in an inscription of Assurbanipal recording his devastation of Elam: "Wild asses, serpents, beasts of the desert … safely I caused to lie down in them." Isaiah may have known of such boasts, and his words point to the law of retribution: the doom Babylon inflicted on others would come upon herself (cf. Psalm 137:8). (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/13.htm)

Modern travellers confirm the fulfillment: "Owls start from the scanty thickets, and the foul jackal stalks among the furrows." (Layard, *Nineveh and Babylon*, quoted by Ellicott — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/13.htm)

---

## POINTS OF TRADITIONAL AND DENOMINATIONAL DIFFERENCE

### Near vs. Far Fulfillment — The Biggest Interpretive Divide

**The double-fulfillment / "prophetic tension" view:** Most traditional commentators (Gill, Ellicott, Pulpit, Matthew Henry, JFB) hold that Isaiah 13 has a near fulfillment in the Medo-Persian conquest of Babylon (539 BC) and also points typologically to the final judgment. The cosmic language of vv. 9–13 is read figuratively for the near fulfillment and literally for the final Day of the Lord. (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/jfb/isaiah/13.htm, https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/13.htm, https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/isaiah/13.htm)

**The literal-futurist view (Dispensational / some Evangelical):** Precept Austin argues that Isaiah 13 has *never been fully fulfilled*. The reasons: (1) the cosmic signs in v. 10 have not occurred in history; (2) Babylon was never destroyed suddenly and totally "like Sodom and Gomorrah" but declined gradually; (3) Revelation 16:19 describes a future judgment on Babylon — implying the city must be rebuilt and rise to prominence again before its final destruction. This view takes Isaiah 13 as primarily eschatological, with only a partial or typological fulfillment in 539 BC. (https://www.preceptaustin.org/isaiah_13_commentary)

**The symbolic/amillennial view:** The ESV Study Bible (cited by Precept Austin) interprets Babylon as "the proud evil that sets the whole world against God" — not necessarily a literal future city but a symbol of the world system opposed to God. Precept Austin rejects this as not addressing the literal statements of the text. (https://www.preceptaustin.org/isaiah_13_commentary)

### Reformed / Baptist (John Piper, Desiring God):

Piper uses Isaiah 13:13 to preach the final eschatological shaking: "There's coming a day, the Day of the Lord, of fierce anger and retribution … and the earth will be shaken out of its place." He connects it to Hebrews 12:25–28 — the removal of all that can be shaken so that only God's unshakeable kingdom remains. The application is pastoral: worship God with reverence and awe, for "our God is a consuming fire." (https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/a-kingdom-that-cannot-be-shaken)

### Pentecostal / Charismatic (David Guzik, Enduring Word):

Guzik reads the passage in the "prophetic tense" — a near and far fulfillment — but emphasizes the pastoral application heavily. The judgment described is the same unrelenting judgment that fell on Jesus at the cross. The hunted gazelle (v. 14) becomes a picture of Christ who "willingly made Himself so." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-13/)

### Older Baptist (Gill):

Gill reads the chapter as a prophecy of the destruction of literal Babylon, "literally understood as a type and exemplar of the destruction of the mystical Babylon, so often spoken of in the book of the Revelation." He takes most of the cosmic language figuratively: the darkening of sun, moon, and stars represents the gloom of the judgment or the fall of kings and nobles. (https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/isaiah/13.htm)

### Anglican (Ellicott):

Ellicott strongly affirms Isaianic authorship against critics, stating that the objection that the prophecy is too specific "implies a view of prophecy which excludes the element of a divinely given foreknowledge; and that view the present writer does not accept." He reads the cosmic language as figurative in its first application. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/13.htm)

---

## WHAT I COULD NOT FIND

- **Methodist / Wesleyan** verse-by-verse treatment of Isaiah 13 from seedbed.com or wesley.nnu.edu.
- **Lutheran** teaching on this chapter from lcms.org or 1517.org.
- **Catholic / Orthodox** commentary (Haydock, New Advent, OCA).
- **Modern critical scholarship** from bibleodyssey.org.
- **NET Bible translation notes** for this chapter.
- **Prosperity / Word of Faith / hyper-grace** teachings applying this chapter (these traditions rarely produce verse-by-verse commentaries on judgment oracles).
